p: I'm Kuzey Aydın. I'm a Windborn. I can talk to the winds, and since Japan, I can fly. Badly. But I can.

Three of the seven great winds live inside me: the North Wind, the Black Wind and the southeast wind of the desert. Mordecai Vane, the man with the hand of gray stone, has two: the Lodos, which his son took from me on Crete, and the Gündoğusu, the wind of the sunrise, which he took from me himself on the top of Mount Fuji, right after I calmed a typhoon with a song.

He found us because of a tracker. He had hidden it in the bracelet his wife gave to his daughter, Vera, before she died. Ela took it out. Vera threw it into the crater of Mount Fuji. Now he can't follow us anymore.
But he doesn't need to. He has moved my grandmother to the Gate of Seven Winds, under the ground in Cappadocia, in the middle of Turkey. He knows I'll come for her.
The score is three to two. Two Keys are left: the Poyraz, the northeast wind, and the Kıble, the south wind.
And Grandma sent me a message, on a wind she borrowed from Mordecai's own stone hand: *Find the serpent of feathers first. Hurry. He is going to Mexico too.*
**Kuzey Aydın,** 11. A Windborn. Three winds. Can fly. Wears his grandmother's blue scarf every day.
**Ela Aydın,** 12. Kuzey's cousin. Keeper of the Clue Book. On the first page, under Grandma's words, she has written Vera's mother's rule.
**Bora Kaya,** 11. Beastspeaker. Carries a raven's feather and a fox's hair in his hat, and a tiny thunder drum around his neck.
**Vera Vane,** 13. Mordecai's daughter. Her bracelet is empty now. She's free.
**Uncle Tarık.** Ela's dad. Archaeologist. Can fly a kite again.
**Grandma Nermin.** The Keeper. Prisoner beside the Gate of Seven Winds. Knitting a scarf.
**Mordecai Vane.** The Gray Hand. Two Keys in his fist. His hand is cracking.
**Vex Vane,** 13. Mordecai's son. His fingers are stone. When the red dot disappeared, he smiled.

From Tokyo to Mexico City is twelve hours on a plane, across the whole Pacific Ocean, the biggest ocean in the world. You fly across a date line, and you arrive before you left. It's the strangest thing. You leave Tokyo on Tuesday evening, and you land in Mexico on Tuesday afternoon. Bora said it meant we got an extra Tuesday for free, and he was going to spend it eating.
We didn't sit next to the toilets this time. Uncle Tarık had finally run out of every kind of airline miles, and Dr. Amira's cousin's tiny airline didn't fly to Mexico. So Vera paid.

"I have money," she said, at the ticket desk in Tokyo, very quietly. She took out a card. A black one. "My father gave me this card when I was ten. For emergencies. He never checks it. He never checks anything I do with money." She looked at the card for a long moment. "I think this is an emergency."
"Vera," said Uncle Tarık. "Are you sure? Won't he know?"
"He'll know," said Vera. "I don't care anymore." She handed the card to the lady at the desk. "Four... no, five tickets to Mexico City, please. Not next to the toilets."

So for the first time in this whole adventure, we sat in proper seats. In the middle of the plane. With a window. And enough legroom that Bora could stretch out his legs, which he did, and kept saying "Look! Look how far my legs go!" until Ela told him to stop.

Vera sat by the window again. She looked out at the ocean for hours. Endless blue, wrinkled like a blanket, sparkling in the sun. Sometimes there were tiny islands, green and white. Sometimes there were ships, so small they looked like grains of rice.
She kept touching her wrist. Where the bracelet was. The empty bracelet, with its little empty silver setting where the gray stone had been.
"Does it feel strange?" I asked her. "Without the stone?"
She thought about it.

"Lighter," she said. "It feels lighter. Like when you take off a backpack you've been carrying all day, and you forgot it was there." She turned the bracelet around on her wrist. "It's still hers. My mom's. It's more hers now. Without his stone in it."
"Get the bad thing out," I said. "And keep the rest."
She smiled. A real one. "Yes."
Somewhere over the middle of the Pacific, in the middle of the night, I woke up.
The plane was dark and humming. Everyone was asleep. Ela had her head on Uncle Tarık's shoulder. Bora was snoring with his mouth open and his crocodile neck pillow over one eye.
I looked out of the window. Far, far below, the ocean was black. Above, there were stars. Millions of them. And across the middle of the sky, the Milky Way, like a river of light.
And I could hear the winds.

Not the winds inside me. The winds outside. The winds of the Pacific. Huge and slow and ancient, sweeping across the biggest ocean in the world, the way they had for millions of years. They didn't talk much. They were too big to talk. They just moved, and hummed, like a giant breathing.
But under them, very faint, I heard something else.
Two winds. Far away. Somewhere ahead of us, in the east.
One warm and wet, like the Mediterranean. One golden, like sunrise.
The Lodos. And the Gündoğusu.
They were crying. Very quietly. Like two kids locked in a cupboard, who have been crying for so long that they're almost too tired to cry anymore.
And they were moving. Toward Mexico. In a stone hand.
*He is going to Mexico too.*
I pressed my forehead against the cold window, and I whispered, "I'm coming. Hold on. I'm coming."
I don't know if they heard me.

chapters.t: Chapter Two: The City in the Sky
p: Mexico City is built on a lake.
Not next to a lake. *On* a lake. Uncle Tarık told us, in the taxi from the airport, his face pressed against the window, his eyes shining.

"Seven hundred years ago," he said, "the Aztecs came here. They were wandering. Looking for a home. And their god told them to build their city where they saw an eagle sitting on a cactus, eating a snake. And they found it! On a little island, in the middle of a huge lake! So they built a city there. On the island. And then they made more islands. And more. And built bridges between them. And canals. Until they had a city floating on the water, bigger than any city in Europe at the time. They called it Tenochtitlan."

"What happened to the lake?" asked Bora, looking out of the window. There was no lake. Just city. Endless city. Buildings and roads and cars and people, stretching away to the mountains on every side.

"The Spanish came," said Uncle Tarık. "And they drained it. Slowly. Over hundreds of years. And built Mexico City on top of it." He sighed. "The ground is still soft. Like a sponge. The whole city is sinking. A little bit every year."
"Sinking?" said Bora, alarmed.
"Very slowly," said Uncle Tarık. "Don't worry. Not today."

Mexico City is also very high up. More than two thousand meters above the sea. Higher than most mountains in Turkey. The air is thin. When you walk up stairs, you get out of breath. When you run, you feel like your lungs are too small.
Bora found this out at the hotel, when he ran up two flights of stairs to see the view from the roof, and had to lie down on the floor at the top for ten minutes.
"I'm dying," he said, from the floor. "Tell my mother I loved her. Tell her I ate my vegetables."
"You didn't eat your vegetables," said Ela.
"Tell her I did."
But the view from the roof was worth it.

Mexico City is enormous. Even bigger than Cairo. Bigger than anything. It spreads out across a huge valley, surrounded by mountains, in every direction, as far as you can see. And on the horizon, to the southeast, there were two volcanoes. Tall and white-capped, side by side, like a giant and a giantess lying down.

"Popocatépetl," said Vera, reading from her phone, carefully, trying to say it right. "And Iztaccíhuatl. In the old legend, they were a warrior and a princess who loved each other. The princess died of sadness when she thought the warrior had died in battle. When he came back and found her, he carried her to the mountains and laid her down, and knelt beside her with a torch, and they both turned into volcanoes. He still watches over her. That's why Popocatépetl smokes. It's his torch."
We all looked at the two volcanoes. The one that was kneeling had a thin plume of smoke rising from its top, white against the blue sky.
"That's the saddest story I've ever heard," said Bora, from the floor.
"It's a love story," said Vera.
"That's what I said," said Bora.
It was December. Nearly Christmas.

I had forgotten. We'd been traveling for so long, through so many places, so many time zones, that I'd completely lost track of the days. But Mexico City hadn't forgotten. The whole city was getting ready.

There were lights everywhere. Strings of colored lights across the streets, in the trees, on the balconies. Giant red flowers called poinsettias in pots on every corner. Little stalls selling sweets and toys and figures of shepherds and angels and donkeys. And piñatas.
Hundreds of piñatas. Hanging from the market stalls, swinging in the wind. Big round ones, covered in colored paper, with seven cones sticking out of them like the points of a star.
"Seven points," said Ela, stopping in front of one. "Like a compass rose."

"The seven points are the seven deadly sins," said the lady who sold them, who spoke a little English. "Pride, greed, anger. You break them with a stick. With your eyes covered. Then the sweets come out. Like good things coming out of bad." She smiled. "Very traditional. For the posadas."
"What are posadas?" asked Bora.

The lady explained. For nine nights before Christmas, people walk through the streets in the evening, carrying candles, singing, going from house to house. At each house, they knock and ask to come in, and the people inside sing back, *No, there's no room.* Until the last house, where they sing, *Come in, come in,* and everyone goes inside and there's food and hot fruit punch and a piñata.
"It's the story of Mary and Joseph looking for a place to stay," said Uncle Tarık. "Before Jesus was born. Nobody would let them in."
"That's sad too," said Bora.
"But in the end someone does," said the lady. "That's the important part. In the end, someone says *come in.*"
That night, we found a posada.

Or it found us. We were walking back to the hotel after dinner (tacos, eleven of them, for Bora; tacos al pastor, with pork cooked on a spinning spit like a Turkish döner, with pineapple on top, which Bora said was "the döner's cousin"), and we turned a corner into a small street, and there it was.

A procession of people walking slowly down the middle of the street. Children and grandmothers and fathers carrying babies. Everyone holding a little candle in a paper cup. Two children at the front dressed as Mary and Joseph, the little girl on a real donkey. And everyone was singing.
We stood on the corner and watched them pass.

A little old lady at the back of the procession saw us. She looked at the five of us, standing there in our winter coats, which were much too warm for Mexico, looking lost. She came over and put a candle into Vera's hand. Then one into mine. Then Ela's, and Bora's, and Uncle Tarık's.
"Ven," she said, smiling. "Come."
So we walked with them.

We didn't know the songs. We didn't understand most of the words. But we walked down the street with our candles, with a crowd of strangers, in the warm dark. At each house, they knocked, and sang, and the people inside sang back. At the last house, the door opened wide, and everyone sang together, and we all went into a courtyard full of lights and food.

There was hot punch, made of guava and cinnamon and sugar cane. There were tamales, little parcels of corn dough wrapped in leaves. There was a huge pot of something spicy and delicious. And there was a piñata, a big one, with seven points, hanging from a rope across the courtyard.
They made Vera hit it.

They put a blindfold on her, and spun her around three times, and gave her a stick. And everyone sang a song about hitting the piñata. And she swung and missed. And swung and missed. Everyone laughed. Then she swung again, as hard as she could.
The piñata burst open. Sweets and fruit and little toys rained down on everyone. All the children screamed and dived for them.

Vera pulled off her blindfold. She was laughing. Really laughing. With her whole face. Standing in the middle of a stranger's courtyard in Mexico, with sweets falling around her, and a crowd of strangers cheering.
The little old lady who had given us the candles came and hugged her.
I looked at Ela. Ela looked at me.
Neither of us said anything. But we were both thinking the same thing.
*In the end, someone says come in.*
On our second morning in Mexico City, Uncle Tarık took us to see what was left of the lake.

"The Aztecs didn't just build a city on the water," he said, in the taxi. "They grew food on it. They made floating gardens. Little islands made of mud and reeds, anchored to the bottom with trees. They grew corn and beans and flowers on them. Thousands of them. And most of the lake is gone now. But one little part is still there."
It was called Xochimilco. (*So-chee-MEEL-co.* Bora said it about thirty times on the way there, until he got it right, and then he kept saying it anyway, because he liked the sound.)
It was a maze of canals. Long, green, quiet canals, winding between little islands covered in trees and flowers and gardens. And on the canals, there were boats.

They're called trajineras. Long, flat wooden boats, painted in the brightest colors you've ever seen. Red and yellow and blue and pink and green. Each one has a little roof, and an arch over the front with a name painted on it in big flowery letters. *Lupita. Rosita. María Elena. El Amor.* A man stands at the back with a long pole and pushes the boat along, slowly, through the green water.
We got into one called *La Esperanza.* Vera translated. It means *Hope.*

It was so peaceful. The boat slid along the canal. Trees hung over the water. Ducks swam past. Other boats went by, full of families having picnics, laughing and singing. Little boats came up alongside us selling things: corn on a stick, flowers, blankets, cold drinks, tacos.
And then a boat came alongside full of mariachis.

There were eight of them. In black suits covered in silver buttons, with huge sombrero hats, with trumpets and violins and guitars. And they played. Right there, next to our boat, loud and happy and beautiful. The trumpets blared. The violins sang. The biggest guitar, a huge round one called a guitarrón, went *bom-bom-bom.*
Bora stood up in the boat and danced. Badly. The boat rocked so much that Uncle Tarık nearly fell in. The mariachis loved him. They played three more songs, just for him.
Then Bora stopped dancing.
He was looking down into the water. At something by the side of the boat.
"Bora?" said Ela.
He knelt down and put his face very close to the green water.
There was something there. Under the surface. Floating, just below, looking up at him.

It was small, about as long as my hand. Pinkish-white. It had a wide flat head and a big smiling mouth and tiny black eyes. And on each side of its head, it had three feathery pink frills sticking out, like a crown. Like a lion's mane. It had four little legs with tiny fingers.
It was smiling. It looked like it was always smiling.
"An axolotl," breathed Vera. "A real one! They only live here! Nowhere else in the world! They're almost extinct!"
The axolotl floated there in the water, smiling up at Bora.
Bora listened.
Then his face changed.

"She says," he said slowly, "that the water is cold. Colder than it should be. Since three days ago. She says the cold is coming from the north. From where the old pyramids are. She says the axolotls are frightened." He listened again. "She says a man with a gray hand walked along the canal, two nights ago, in a fog. And the water froze where he walked. And some of her cousins froze in the ice. And they're asleep now. And she doesn't know if they'll wake up."
The mariachis had stopped playing. The boat was very quiet.
The axolotl looked up at Bora with its tiny black eyes, and its permanent smile, which didn't look like a smile at all anymore.
"Tell her," I said quietly, "that we'll stop him."
Bora told her.
The axolotl floated there for a moment longer. Then it turned, very slowly, and swam away into the green water, its feathery pink frills waving.
Nobody said anything for a long time.
"Even the axolotls," said Ela at last. "He's hurting everything. Everywhere he goes. Even things he doesn't know exist."

The boatman pushed his long pole into the water, and *La Esperanza* slid on down the canal. The mariachis played a slow song, a sad one. And I sat at the front of the boat, and watched the green water, and thought about the little frozen axolotls asleep in the ice.
And I made another promise. Very quietly. To nobody. To the wind.
There was a tiny drawing next to the star on the leather map. There always was. A split rock in Iceland. A gate and a fox in Japan.
In Mexico, it was a head. A snake's head, with feathers around its neck, like a lion's mane. And beside it, the smallest drawing of all: a kite. A kite with seven tails.

"A feathered serpent," said Uncle Tarık. "Quetzalcoatl. The great god of the Aztecs, and the Toltecs, and the people before them. A god of wind, and wisdom, and learning. In his wind form, he was called Ehecatl. He wore a mask with a long red beak, like a duck, so he could blow the wind. He swept the roads clear so the rain gods could come."
"And the kite?" said Ela.
Nobody knew.
So we asked the wind.

The wind in Mexico was hot and dry, even in December, and full of stories. It talked fast, like a market seller, jumping from one thing to another, never finishing a sentence before starting the next one.

*Hello hello, Windborn, welcome, welcome! So many visitors! The kite? The kite man! Of course, of course! The old kite man in Coyoacán! By the coyote fountain! Nermin's friend! Go, go, go, he's waiting, he's been waiting forty years, he's very old now, very old, hurry!*

Coyoacán is an old part of Mexico City, with cobbled streets and colorful houses painted blue and yellow and pink, and big trees, and a square with a fountain in the middle shaped like two coyotes. We found the fountain easily.
And next to it, under a tree, an old man was selling kites.

He was very old. Older than Rıza Usta. Older than Guðrún. He had a brown, wrinkled face, like a walnut, and white hair, and a big straw hat. He sat on a little wooden stool, with dozens of kites hanging from the branches of the tree around him. Paper kites, painted with birds and suns and stars and skulls with flowers. They fluttered and danced in the breeze.
And one kite, hanging from the very top branch, was different from the others.

It was shaped like a snake. A long, thin snake, made of green paper, with a head covered in green and gold feathers. And it had seven tails. Seven long ribbons, each a different color, streaming out behind it.
The old man looked up as we came toward him. He looked at Uncle Tarık, and Ela, and Bora, and Vera.
Then he looked at me.
He didn't say anything for a long time. He just looked. His dark eyes went very wide.
Then he stood up, slowly, and took off his hat, and held it against his chest.
"Por fin," he said softly. "At last."
His name was Don Tomás. He was ninety-four years old. And he had been a member of the Order of the Compass Rose for seventy-six years.

"I sell kites," he said, in slow, careful English, sitting us down on the edge of the coyote fountain. "Every day. For sixty years. In this square. Because Nermin told me, forty years ago, 'Tomás, one day a boy will come who can fly without a kite. Wait for him by the kites. He will find you.'" He laughed, a dry, wheezing laugh. "Forty years I sit here, waiting. Selling kites to children. My wife said I was crazy. She was right. But I was also right."
He reached up, very slowly, into the branches of the tree, and took down the green feathered snake kite with seven tails.
"For you," he said. "From Nermin. She made it. With her own hands. Forty years ago."
I took it. It was light as air. The paper was old and soft, but the colors were still bright. And when the breeze touched it, the seven tails lifted and danced.
On the back of the snake's head, in tiny writing, in pencil, there were words. In Turkish. In Grandma's handwriting.
*Where the gods were born, the serpent sleeps beneath its own temple. Follow the road of the dead to the house of a hundred heads. Go down where the stars are underground.*
§CLUE The serpent of feathers sleeps beneath the city of the gods. Go down the road of the dead, to the temple of a hundred heads, where the stars are underground.

chapters.t: Chapter Six: The City of the Gods
p: "The city of the gods," said Don Tomás, "is Teotihuacan."
He said it slowly. *Teh-oh-tee-wah-KAHN.* Bora tried to say it and got it wrong four times. Don Tomás laughed his wheezing laugh and said Bora's fifth try was "almost Aztec."

"It is an hour from here," he said. "To the north. An old, old city. Older than the Aztecs. Much older. When the Aztecs found it, it was already ruins. Already empty. Nobody knew who built it. So the Aztecs said, *the gods built it.* They said it was where the gods were born. Where the sun and the moon were made." He pointed at the clue on the kite. "And there is a road there. A long, straight road, through the middle of the city. The Aztecs called it the Avenue of the Dead. Because they thought the buildings beside it were tombs."
"The road of the dead," said Ela, writing.
"And at the end of the road," said Don Tomás, "there is a temple. The Temple of the Feathered Serpent. Its walls are covered in heads. Hundreds of stone heads. Serpents with feathers. Like the kite."
"The house of a hundred heads," I said.
"And 'where the stars are underground'?" asked Vera.
Don Tomás's face went serious.

"Twenty years ago," he said, "the archaeologists found a tunnel. Under the Temple of the Feathered Serpent. Very deep. Very long. Nobody knew it was there for fifteen hundred years. It took them ten years to dig it out. And inside..." He shook his head slowly. "Treasures. Thousands of them. Jade. Shells. Seeds. Little statues. And the walls of the tunnel, they were covered in a special stone. Pyrite. Fool's gold. It sparkles. When the ancient people carried torches down there, the walls sparkled like a sky full of stars." He looked at me. "An underground sky. Where the stars are underground."

Uncle Tarık was making little excited noises. "I read about it! In a journal! The tunnel under the Feathered Serpent! They found pools of liquid mercury at the bottom! Mercury, Kuzey! A metal that's liquid! Silver pools! Nobody knows why it was there! They think it was meant to look like an underground river! Or a lake! The lake of the underworld!"
"Mercury is poisonous," said Ela sharply. "Very poisonous. You can't touch it. You can't even breathe it, if it's warm."
"Yes," said Don Tomás quietly. "That is true."
There was a long silence. The kites rustled in the tree above us.

"And there is something else," said Don Tomás. "Something the archaeologists did not find. At the very end of the tunnel, there are three rooms. The archaeologists found them empty." He smiled a little. "But they did not know how to look. There is a fourth room. Behind the third. Nermin showed me, forty years ago, before the archaeologists came. We went down there together, by candlelight, with a rope. And she showed me." He tapped the kite gently. "The serpent sleeps there. The real one. Not a statue."
"The real Feathered Serpent?" said Bora.
"Ehecatl," said Don Tomás. "The wind that sweeps the road for the rain."
He looked toward the north, where the sky was turning orange with the sunset.

"Go tomorrow," he said. "At dawn. Early. Very early." He lowered his voice. "Because the gray men came to the city three days ago. Many of them. And last night, my grandson saw a man walking out of the fog by the airport. A tall man, in a long gray coat. With a boy beside him."
The kites in the tree above us stopped rustling. All at once. As if they had heard.
"Your enemy is already here," said Don Tomás.

chapters.t: Chapter Seven: Meanwhile, in the Fog
p: *Vex told Kuzey about this, much later.*
His father was coughing.

They had come out of the fog road at the edge of Mexico City, in the middle of the night, in a field of tall dry grass next to the airport. Planes were roaring overhead. The fog clung around them, cold and gray, and then slowly drained away into the warm air like water into sand.
And his father bent over, with his hands on his knees, and coughed. And coughed. A deep, painful, rattling cough, that went on for a whole minute.
Vex stood there and didn't know what to do.
He had never seen his father like this. His father was never sick. Never tired. Never weak. His father was cold and strong and perfect, always.
"Father?" he said.
Mordecai straightened up slowly. He wiped his mouth with his human hand, his left one. His face was gray in the moonlight. Grayer than it should have been.
"It's nothing," he said. "The fog road. It's longer, this one. All the way across the ocean. It takes more out of you."
But Vex had seen his stone hand, when he was coughing. Clenched around the two Keys. The Lodos and the Gündoğusu.

The cracks had spread again. Up past his wrist now. Onto his arm. Gray and dry and cracked, like old clay. And when his father moved his fingers, little bits of stone fell off and drifted away on the wind.

And the Keys were screaming. Both of them. Vex could hear them clearly now, even when he wasn't standing close. Two thin, high screams, one warm and one golden, like two kettles boiling on a stove that nobody would turn off.
"They're fighting you," Vex said quietly. "The winds. Aren't they? They're fighting to get out."
His father didn't answer. He started walking. Toward the lights of the city.
Vex followed him.

"Tomorrow," said Mordecai, without turning around, "you will go to Teotihuacan. Before the boy. You will go down into the tunnel under the Feathered Serpent. And you will find the Poyraz. And you will take it." He paused. "Do you understand? *You* will take it. Not the boy. You."
"Yes, Father."
"I can't hold another one," said Mordecai. Very quietly. So quietly that Vex almost didn't hear. "Not yet. Not until the Gate. My hand can't..." He stopped. He didn't finish.
Vex looked down at his own hands. His stone fingers. Past the knuckles now, on both hands. Gray and hard, clicking when he moved them.
He understood.
His father couldn't hold another Key. So Vex would have to.
In his own stone hand.
He walked behind his father through the tall grass, toward the city, with the planes roaring over his head. And for the first time in his whole life, Vex Vane thought: *I don't want to.*
He thought it very quietly. So quietly that even he could barely hear it.
But he thought it.

chapters.t: Chapter Eight: The Pyramid of the Sun
p: We left the hotel at four in the morning, in the dark, in a taxi driven by Don Tomás's grandson. His name was Rodrigo. He was about twenty, with long hair and a big grin, and he drove so fast that Uncle Tarık spent the whole journey with his eyes closed, saying prayers in three languages.

Don Tomás had wanted to come. Rodrigo wouldn't let him. "Abuelo," he said firmly. "You are ninety-four. You stay home. You sell kites." Don Tomás grumbled a lot. But he gave me a hug before we left, a dry, bony hug that smelled of paper and paint, and he whispered, "Tell Nermin the kites are still flying."
We reached Teotihuacan just as the sky was getting light.
And I stopped. In the car park. With my mouth open.
I had seen the pyramids of Egypt. I thought nothing could ever be as amazing as that. But this was different. Not better. Different.

The city of the gods spread out in front of us in the gray dawn light. Huge and silent and empty. A long, wide, straight road ran through the middle of it, straight as a ruler, stretching away for kilometers, all the way to the mountains on the horizon. On both sides of the road, there were platforms and steps and ruined buildings, gray and brown, with grass growing between the stones.
And rising above everything, on the right side of the road, was a pyramid.
The Pyramid of the Sun.

It was huge. Not as tall as the Great Pyramid in Egypt, but wider. Much wider. And it wasn't smooth, or pointed. It was built in steps. Five great levels, one on top of another, like a giant's staircase, with a steep stone stairway running up the middle of the front, all the way to the flat top.
And at the far end of the long road, at the very end, in front of the mountains, there was another one. Smaller. The Pyramid of the Moon.

"The Sun and the Moon," said Uncle Tarık softly. He had opened his eyes. "The Aztecs believed that this is where the gods made the sun and the moon. At the beginning of the world. Two gods jumped into a great fire, here, and one came out as the sun, and one came out as the moon."
"Can we climb it?" said Bora. He was looking up at the Pyramid of the Sun. At the long, long, steep stairway going up and up.
"No," said Ela. "We don't have time. The temple's at the other end."
"I wasn't asking because I *wanted* to," said Bora. "I was asking because I'm scared of heights, and I wanted to know if I had to."
"You don't have to," said Ela.
"Thank you," said Bora.
But I did climb it.
Just me. Not up the stairs. I flew.

Very early, while the others waited at the bottom. While there was nobody else there. Just a short flight, up the side of the pyramid, wobbling a bit, in the cold dawn air. Rodrigo stood in the car park with his mouth open. And I landed on the flat top of the Pyramid of the Sun just as the sun came up.

It rose over the mountains in the east, huge and orange. And the light poured across the city of the gods. Across the long straight road. Across the platforms and the ruins and the pyramids. Turning everything gold.

From the top of the pyramid, I could see the whole city. And I could see that it wasn't random. It was a pattern. Everything lined up. Everything pointed. The road. The pyramids. The mountains. Like a giant compass, laid out on the ground.
And the wind came up the side of the pyramid, hot and dry and full of stories, and said:
*Look, Windborn. Look at the end of the road. Look at the temple.*
I looked.

At the far end of the long straight road, to the south, there was a huge square courtyard, surrounded by walls. And in the middle of it, a temple. A stepped temple, like the pyramid, but smaller. And even from here, I could see that its walls were strange. Lumpy. Covered in shapes.
Heads.
And in front of the temple, very small, there were people. Standing in a group. Not tourists. It was much too early for tourists.
Gray people.

chapters.t: Chapter Nine: The Avenue of the Dead
p: I flew back down. Badly. I landed in a bush. Rodrigo helped me out.
"Grays," I said, as soon as I could breathe. "At the temple. Already. Lots of them."
Vera's face went hard. "Then we need to move."

The Avenue of the Dead is long. Very long. More than two kilometers. It's straight and wide and paved with old stones, and it goes slightly uphill, so walking down it feels like walking into the past. On both sides, there are stone platforms, with stairs going up to the top, where temples once stood. They're mostly ruins now. Gray stone and grass. Lizards sunning themselves. Cactus plants growing in the cracks.
It was hot already. So hot. The sun was up, and it was blazing down on the stones, and the air above the road wobbled like water. After the snow of Mount Fuji, it felt like walking into an oven.
Bora had already drunk three bottles of water and was eyeing a man setting up a stall at the side of the road, selling mango slices with chili powder.
"No," said Ela.
"I didn't say anything."
"You were thinking it."
"Thinking isn't a crime," said Bora.
The wind was talking to me the whole way. Hot and dry and fast, jumping from one thing to another.

*Hello hello, Windborn, welcome, welcome! So many visitors today! The gray one came last night. Yes, yes. With his cold hand and his gray men. Not him. Not the man. The boy. The boy came. With the gray men. He is digging, digging. Under the feathered temple. You are late, little one. But maybe not too late. Maybe. Maybe not. Hurry!*
"Vex," I said. "It's Vex. Not his father."
Vera's face changed. Something flickered across it. Worry. Fear.
For her brother.
We walked faster.

The avenue went on and on. Past the Pyramid of the Sun, huge and golden in the morning light. Past more platforms. Past a little river, crossing the road in a stone channel. Bora's legs were getting tired. Uncle Tarık was getting pink in the face. Ela was walking very fast, with her head down, not talking. Vera was walking even faster.
And I was listening. To the wind. To the Grays. To the faint sound, coming from somewhere ahead, deep under the ground, of digging.
And under the digging, something else.
A breath. A slow, deep, warm breath, coming up out of the earth. In. And out. In. And out.
Something under the temple was breathing.

chapters.t: Chapter Ten: The Temple of a Hundred Heads
p: The Temple of the Feathered Serpent was at the far end of the avenue, inside a huge square courtyard surrounded by walls of stone. The courtyard was so big that you could have fitted ten football fields inside it. The walls were wide and flat on top, with stairs going up them, like seats in a stadium.
In the middle of the courtyard stood the temple.
It was a stepped pyramid, like the others. But it was covered in heads.

Giant stone heads, sticking out of the walls, one after another, in rows, on every level. Snakes. Huge serpent heads, with their mouths wide open, showing big stone fangs. And around each head, a ring of carved feathers, spreading out like a lion's mane. Between the serpent heads, there were other heads. Strange, square faces, with round goggle eyes, like masks.

There were hundreds of them. All staring out at us across the courtyard with their blank stone eyes. Some of them still had paint on them, after nearly two thousand years. Faint traces of red and blue and green.
"The house of a hundred heads," whispered Ela.
There were no tourists. A rope with a sign blocked the entrance to the courtyard: CERRADO. Closed.
And standing in front of the temple, with their backs to us, were six men in gray suits.
We crouched down behind the wall at the edge of the courtyard. Peering over the top.
"Grays," whispered Ela. "Six of them."
"I count seven," whispered Bora. "There's one sleeping in the shade. Over there. By that pillar."

He was right. One Gray was sitting on the ground with his back against a stone, in the shade, with his head on his chest. Asleep. I didn't know Grays could sleep. It made them seem a tiny bit more human.

The Grays were standing around a hole in the ground. At the foot of the temple, right in front of the great stone stairway. A dark square hole, with a ladder going down. Next to it was a big pile of dirt and some shovels and a wheelbarrow.
"The tunnel," whispered Uncle Tarık. His eyes were shining, even now. "The tunnel under the temple. The archaeologists closed it up again, years ago. They've opened it."
"Vex is down there," said Vera. Very quietly. "I know he is."
"How do we get past seven Grays?" said Ela.
Nobody had an answer.

Then Bora reached into his shirt and pulled out the tiny drum on its red cord. The one Raijin had given him on the top of Mount Fuji. Round and red, small enough to fit in his palm, with a tiny drumstick tied to it.
He looked at me.
*When animals are needed, beat it once. Only once. They will hear it across a thousand miles.*
"Do it," I said.
Bora held the little drum in his palm. He took the tiny drumstick in his other hand. He closed his eyes.
"Please," he whispered. "Anyone who can hear me. We need help. The gray men. Please chase them away. Just for a little while. Don't hurt them. Just chase them."
He tapped the drum once with the tiny stick.
*Tum.*
It made almost no sound. A tiny, soft *tum,* like a drop of rain on a leaf.
Nothing happened.
We waited. The Grays stood around the hole. The sleeping Gray snored. The sun blazed down on the courtyard.
"Maybe it didn't work," whispered Ela.
Then the ground started to buzz.

At first, I thought it was my imagination. A tiny hum. Like a fridge. Coming from the stones under our feet. Then louder. From the walls of the courtyard. From the grass. From the cracks in the ancient stones. From the cactus plants. From everywhere.
And then came the bees.

Thousands of them. Maybe millions. Pouring out of the cracks and the walls and the ground, out of holes I didn't even know were there, a golden-brown cloud, buzzing so loudly that the air itself seemed to shake. They swirled up into the sky over the courtyard like smoke. Then they dived.

After the bees came the birds. Swallows and sparrows and grackles, black and shiny, screaming. Big black vultures, circling low, with their wings spread wide. A hawk. Two hawks. A flock of bright green parrots, from somewhere, shrieking.
And after the birds, slowly, came a lizard.

A very large lizard. An iguana. As long as Bora's arm, with spikes down its back, and a big flap of skin under its chin, and a very confused expression. It walked out from behind a stone, stopped in the middle of the courtyard, and looked around, as if it was wondering why it had come.
The Grays screamed.

All of them. Even Grays, it turns out, scream when attacked by a million bees and a lot of angry birds. They ran. In every direction. Waving their arms. Swatting at the bees. Covering their heads from the birds. The sleeping Gray woke up, saw the iguana right in front of his face, and screamed loudest of all, and ran fastest of all.
In about thirty seconds, the courtyard was empty. Except for us. And the iguana.
The bees were still buzzing, chasing the Grays out across the Avenue of the Dead, a golden cloud following them. We could hear the screaming getting farther away.
"What," whispered Ela, "did you *say* to them?"

"I just said please chase the gray men for ten minutes," said Bora. He was staring at the drum in his hand. "The bees said it would be their pleasure. They said they've never liked the gray men. They said the gray men make the flowers cold."
The iguana walked slowly over to Bora. It looked up at him.
Bora listened.

"He says," said Bora, "he isn't sure why he's here. He says he heard a drum, and felt he should come. He says he isn't very good at chasing things." Bora knelt down. "That's okay," he told the iguana. "You can just stay here and look after the entrance. Can you do that?"
The iguana thought about it. Then it walked slowly over to the hole in the ground, and lay down next to the ladder, in the sun, and closed its eyes.
"He says he's very good at that," said Bora.

chapters.t: Chapter Twelve: The Tunnel of Stars
p: The tunnel under the temple was narrow, and low, and very, very long.

The ladder went down about fifteen meters, straight down, into the dark. At the bottom, a tunnel went off sideways, under the temple. It was carved out of the rock, rough and bumpy. Just high enough to walk through bent over, at first. Then lower. Then so low that we had to crawl.
Uncle Tarık went first, with his flashlight. The right way up, this time. Then Ela. Then Vera. Then me. Then Bora, at the back, because he said if he got stuck, he didn't want to block anyone.
He didn't get stuck. But it was close a few times.

The tunnel went down. Slowly. Always down. Deeper and deeper under the city of the gods. It smelled of earth and stone and very old air. Air that hadn't moved for fifteen hundred years. It was cool after the heat outside. Then cold.
And the walls sparkled.

In the light of the flashlight, the walls of the tunnel glittered. Tiny points of light, everywhere, in the rock. Thousands of them. Gold and silver, flashing as the light moved over them. Like stars.

"Pyrite," whispered Uncle Tarık, stopping to look. "Fool's gold. The ancient people ground it up and mixed it with clay and covered the walls with it. With torches, the whole tunnel would have glittered like a sky full of stars."
"An underground sky," said Ela softly. "Where the stars are underground. So the tunnel is like a map of the stars. Of the underworld."

"The Aztecs believed in an underworld," said Uncle Tarık. "Mictlan. Nine levels, deep under the earth. When you died, your soul had to travel down through all nine. Through rivers and mountains and winds made of knives. It took four years."
"Winds made of knives?" said Bora, from the back. "Why is it always the scary stuff? Why don't they ever have a nice underworld? With snacks?"
"I'll make you a nice underworld when we get home," said Ela. "With snacks."
"Thank you," said Bora.
The wind came with us. A little hot breath, at our backs, from the opening far behind us. Whispering. Guiding.
*Left, little one. Now right. Careful. Careful. The boy is ahead. He is close. And something is breathing.*

We crawled for what felt like an hour. My knees hurt. My back hurt. My hands were scraped and dusty. Bora was breathing very loudly behind me, the way he does when he's trying not to be scared of the dark.
"You okay, Bora?" I whispered.
"I'm fine," he whispered back. "I'm fine. I'm fine. I'm fine."
Then the tunnel opened up.
And Uncle Tarık, at the front, stopped so suddenly that Ela crashed into him.
"Don't move," he said. His voice was very quiet. Very calm. Too calm. "Nobody move."

chapters.t: Chapter Thirteen: The Lake of Silver
p: We were in a cave. Not big. About the size of a classroom. With a low, glittering ceiling, covered in pyrite stars. And the whole floor of the cave was a lake.
A lake of silver.

It was liquid. It moved, slowly, in little ripples, when the warm wind breathed across it. But it wasn't water. It was too bright. Too shiny. It reflected the flashlight like a mirror. Like liquid metal. It looked heavy. Thick. Like melted silver. Like the silver line inside an old thermometer, but a whole lake of it.
"Mercury," said Uncle Tarık. Very quietly.
"Poisonous," said Ela. Even more quietly. "Very poisonous. Don't touch it. Don't breathe near it. Dad, it's warm in here. Warm mercury makes a gas."
We all stepped back. Very, very carefully.

On the other side of the silver lake, about ten meters away, there was an opening in the rock. A dark doorway. And from it came the warm breathing. In and out. In and out. And the faint sound of someone moving. Someone digging.
"Vex," whispered Vera. "He's through there."
"How did he get across?" said Bora.
We looked. The lake went all the way from wall to wall. There was no path around it. No bridge.
Then Ela pointed with the flashlight.
There were stones. Sticking up out of the silver lake. Flat stones, round, about the size of dinner plates. In a line. Going across the lake to the doorway on the other side. Stepping stones.
"Of course," said Bora. "Of course there are stepping stones. Why wouldn't there be stepping stones over a lake of poison?"
"There are a lot of them," said Vera. She was counting. "Twenty-one. Too many. They're not in a straight line. They're all over the place. Some of them must be wrong."
"Like the floor of letters in Crete," I said.
Ela was looking at the stones very carefully. Her eyes moved fast, back and forth.
"Each stone has a picture on it," she said. "Look."
She was right. Carved into the top of each stone, very faint, there was a little picture. A sun. A moon. A rabbit. A deer. A snake. A jaguar. An eagle. A flower. Lots of different pictures.

"Aztec day signs," said Uncle Tarık. "From their calendar. They had twenty day signs. Each day was named after one. Crocodile, Wind, House, Lizard, Serpent, Death, Deer, Rabbit, Water, Dog, Monkey, Grass, Reed, Jaguar, Eagle, Vulture, Movement, Flint, Rain, Flower."
"Wind," said Ela immediately. "Is there a sign for wind?"
"Ehecatl," said Uncle Tarık. "The second day sign. Wind. It's a face. With a mask. With a long beak. Like a duck."
Ela's flashlight moved across the stones. Sun. Rabbit. Flower. Eagle.
Duck face.
"There!" said Ela. "First one, there! On the left!"
And then the next one, two stones further on. A duck face. And the next. Zigzagging across the silver lake, from stone to stone, all the way to the doorway on the other side. Seven of them.
"Seven," said Ela. "Of course. Seven duck faces. Seven winds."
§CLUE Across the lake of silver, step only on the stones carved with the Aztec day sign for Wind: a face wearing a mask with a long beak. There are seven.
"I'll go first," I said.
"No," said Vera.
We all looked at her.

"I'll go first," she said. "He's my brother." She looked at the silver lake, and the stones, and the dark doorway on the other side. "And if anything happens to anyone, it's going to be me. Not you. You have to get to the Gate. You have to get your grandmother. I don't have anyone waiting for me."
"Vera..." said Ela.
But she had already stepped onto the first stone.
Vera stepped onto the first duck face.
The stone wobbled a little under her foot. The silver lake rippled around it, slow and heavy, like syrup. She stood there, very still, with her arms out for balance.
Nothing happened.
She stepped onto the second. Two stones ahead, to the right. It was a long step. She had to stretch. The silver lake shone underneath her, reflecting her face, upside down.
Nothing happened.

The third. The fourth. She didn't look back. She didn't look down. She kept her eyes on the next stone, and stepped, and balanced, and stepped again. Her face was white in the light of the flashlight. Her lips were pressed together.
The fifth.
"Careful," whispered Ela. "The sixth is a long way. To the left."
Vera looked at the sixth stone. It was far. Much farther than the others. Almost a jump.
She jumped.
She landed on it. It wobbled. She wobbled. Her arms went out wide. For one terrible second, she leaned out over the silver lake, so far that her hair almost touched the surface.
Then she caught her balance.
Nobody breathed.
The seventh. A small step. Then the rock floor on the other side. Then she was across, standing in the dark doorway, turning around to look back at us. She was shaking all over.
"It's okay," she called, very quietly. "It's safe. Come on. Follow the ducks."

Ela went next. She went fast, the way she does everything, light and quick, with her braids swinging. She didn't even stop on the sixth stone. She just jumped from the fifth to the seventh, missing out the sixth completely, and landed next to Vera.
"Show-off," said Vera, and Ela grinned.

Uncle Tarık went next. Very, very slowly. He said something in Latin on every single stone. Ela said later it was a prayer to the patron saint of archaeologists. Uncle Tarık said it was the scientific name for mercury. Either way, he got across.

Then me. I could have flown. But I didn't. It didn't feel right. The stones were there for a reason. So I stepped on them, one by one, the way Vera had. And on each one, I felt something. A little warmth, coming up through my feet. Like the stone was saying *yes. Yes. This way.*
Then Bora.
Bora stood on the edge of the silver lake and looked at the first stone for a long time.
"Bora?" I said. "You can do it."
"I know I can do it," said Bora. "I'm just thinking about how much I don't want to."
He was afraid. I could see it. The dark, the depth, and now a lake of poison. And he was the heaviest of all of us. The stones were small.
"Bora," said Vera, from the doorway. "Look at me. Not at the lake. Look at me. And step."
Bora looked at her.
And he stepped.
One. Two. Three. Four. Looking at Vera the whole time. Not at the stones. Not at the silver. Just at her face. Five. The sixth stone, the far one. He looked at it. He looked at Vera.
"Jump," she said.
He jumped.

He landed on the sixth stone so hard that it sank. Just a little. One centimeter. The silver lake slopped up over the edge of it, and for a second, the mercury was touching the side of his shoe, shining.
"BORA!" screamed Ela.

He jumped again. To the seventh. Then onto the rock floor. And we all grabbed him, and pulled him into the doorway, and Ela pulled his shoe off and threw it back into the lake, where it sank slowly into the silver and disappeared.
Bora stood there with one shoe on and one sock, breathing very hard.
"That was my favorite shoe," he said.
"You can have mine," said Vera. "When we get out."
"Your feet are tiny."
"Then I'll buy you a new one," said Vera. "A better one."
Bora looked at her. Then he nodded. "Okay," he said. "Thank you. For looking at me."
"That's what my mother did," said Vera quietly. "When I was scared. She said, 'Don't look at the scary thing. Look at me.'"

chapters.t: Chapter Fifteen: The Chamber of Treasures
p: The doorway led into a round chamber with a low ceiling.

On the floor, little stone figures lay everywhere. Hundreds of them. Tiny people, carved from green stone, with their arms by their sides. Tiny animals: dogs and birds and jaguars. Shells, from the sea, hundreds of kilometers away. Balls of black rubber. Pots. Knives made of shiny black glass. And beads. Hundreds and hundreds of beads made of green stone, scattered across the floor like seeds.
"Offerings," whispered Uncle Tarık. "To the gods. Fifteen hundred years old." He looked like he might cry. "Nobody has seen these. Nobody. Not even the archaeologists."
In the middle of the chamber was a hole.

A deep, round pit. Going straight down into darkness. About as wide as a car. Its edges were smooth, worn down by something. By wind, maybe. Or water. Or time. From deep, deep down inside it came the breathing. Warm and slow. In and out. Much louder now. Like a giant, sleeping at the bottom of a well.
And on the far side of the pit, on a narrow stone ledge that ran along the wall, stood Vex Vane.

He was alone. No Grays. Just him. He was covered in dust, his clothes torn, his face dirty and scratched. His gray gloves were on. And he was reaching up toward the ceiling of the chamber, stretching as high as he could, on his tiptoes, on the narrow ledge.
Toward something glowing.

High in the ceiling, above the pit, there was a bronze needle. Stuck into the rock, as if someone had thrown it there like a dart. It glowed a soft green, like new leaves. And around it, carved into the ceiling, were feathers. Long, curving stone feathers, spreading out from the needle like rays of light. Painted green, still, after fifteen hundred years.
The Poyraz Key.
The northeast wind. The great wind of the Black Sea. The wind of my own city. The wind that was blowing on the day Grandma disappeared.
"Vex!" said Vera.
He turned so fast that he almost fell off the ledge.

When he saw his sister, something flashed in his eyes. In the light of the flashlight, across the pit. Anger, first. Then something else. Something that looked like relief. Then something that looked like fear.
"Go away, Vera," he said. His voice was hoarse. He'd been down here a long time. "He's coming. He sent me ahead to get it. He's coming down himself, soon. If he finds you here..."
"He won't hurt me," said Vera.

"He froze the professor in Crete," said Vex. "He froze half of Iceland. He put a *tracker* in Mom's bracelet." His voice cracked on the last word. "Do you really think he won't hurt you? Do you really still think that?"
Vera didn't answer.

"He doesn't care about us," said Vex. His face was twisted. "Not anymore. He only cares about the Gate. That's all. That's all there is. The Gate and the Keys and the winds." He held up his gloved hands. "Look what he's done to me, Vera. *Look.*"
He pulled off one of his gloves.
His hand underneath was stone. Not just the fingertips anymore. The whole hand. Gray and hard and cracked, all the way to his wrist. Like his father's. Exactly like his father's.
Vera made a sound. A small, terrible sound.

"He wants me to hold the Key," said Vex. "In this. Because his hand can't hold any more. So I have to. And then my hand will be like his. All the way up. Forever." He looked at his stone hand. "I don't want to, Vera. I don't want to."
Then the ledge under his feet broke.
It happened so fast.
One second, Vex was standing on the ledge. The next, the stone crumbled under him like dry bread. There was a crack, and a rattle, and a puff of dust.
And he was falling.
Falling into the black pit, his arms reaching up, his stone hand and his gloved hand clawing at the air, his mouth open in a scream that echoed round and round the stone walls.
Vera screamed his name.
I didn't think.
I jumped.
I didn't decide to. I didn't plan it. My legs just did it, before my brain could catch up. I ran three steps and jumped off the edge of the pit, into the dark, after Vex.
Behind me, Ela screamed my name. I felt Uncle Tarık's hand grab for my shirt. Miss it by a centimeter. I heard Bora shout something that wasn't words at all.
And then I was falling too.
Into the dark.

It was black. Completely black. The flashlight was far above me now, a tiny circle of light, getting smaller. The walls of the pit rushed past. Cold air rushed up past my face. And somewhere below me, in the dark, I could hear Vex screaming.
*Let go of the ground,* said Sōjōbō, in my head. *Trust the wind.*
There was no ground. There was nothing to hold on to. Only the dark. Only the falling.
So I trusted the wind.
*Wind,* I thought. *Please. Please. Please.*
And the three winds inside me burst out all at once.

The North Wind, freezing and sharp and bright. The Black Wind, wild and dark and stormy. The Keşişleme, hot as the desert at noon. They came out of me in a rush, all three together, and they wrapped around me, and they caught me. Like a hand. Like a net. Like a hammock.
I stopped falling.
And I reached down. Into the darkness. Blindly. With my whole arm, as far as it would go.
And my fingers closed around a wrist.
A stone wrist. Hard and cold and cracked.
I held on.

We stopped. Both of us. Hanging in the air, in the middle of the dark pit, halfway down. Vex dangling from my hand, his feet kicking in the empty dark. Me floating above him, held up by three winds, my arm stretched so far that it felt like it would come out of its socket.
Below us, very far down, I could hear water. Rushing water. An underground river. And the warm breathing, louder than ever, coming up from the depths.
Vex stared up at me.
In the faint light from the flashlight, far above, I could see his face. White. Shocked. His green eyes huge.
"Why?" he gasped. "Why would you do that?"
"Hold on," I said through my teeth. "Just hold on."
"I tried to *freeze* you!" Vex's voice was high and cracking. "On the tower! I took your Key! I froze your uncle! I grabbed your cousin! I chased you across half the world! *Why?*"
"I know," I said.

My arm was shaking. Holding two people up with wind is much, much harder than holding one. The winds inside me were straining. I could feel them, pushing up with everything they had. The North Wind was cold with effort. The Black Wind was crackling. The Keşişleme had stopped talking completely, which it never does.
"You're still a person, Vex," I said. "That's why. People don't deserve to fall in holes. Not even you."
The winds lifted us. Slowly. So slowly.
Up through the dark. A centimeter at a time. My arm was screaming. My shoulder was on fire. Vex's stone wrist was cold and slippery in my hand. I could feel it sliding. I gripped harder.
"Don't let go," Vex whispered. "Please don't let go."
"I won't," I said.
Up. And up. The circle of light above us getting bigger. I could see faces now. Peering over the edge. Ela. Vera. Bora. Uncle Tarık.
"KUZEY!" Ela was screaming. "KUZEY, HOLD ON!"
Up. Up.
"Almost," Bora was shouting. "Almost! Come on! Come on!"
The edge of the pit. Right there. A meter above us. Half a meter.
Bora reached down.

He lay on his stomach on the edge of the pit, with Uncle Tarık holding his legs, and Ela holding Uncle Tarık, and he reached down into the dark with both his huge arms. And he grabbed Vex. Under the arms. And pulled.

Bora is the strongest person I know. He pulled Vex up out of that pit like he was pulling a bag of shopping out of a car. One big heave, and Vex was out, and lying on the stone floor of the chamber, gasping.
Then Bora reached down again. And grabbed me. And pulled.
And I was out too. Lying on my back on the cold stone floor, among the little green statues and the shells and the beads, staring up at the glittering ceiling.
I couldn't move my arm. I couldn't move anything. My whole body was shaking.
Ela was on her knees next to me. She was crying. Again. She grabbed my good hand.
"You *idiot,*" she said. "You complete, total, absolute *idiot.* You jumped into a *pit!* A *bottomless pit!* For *him!*"
"It wasn't bottomless," I said weakly. "There was a river."
Ela made a sound that was half a laugh and half a sob, and hit me on the shoulder. My bad shoulder. I yelped.
"Sorry," she said. "Sorry, sorry, sorry."
On the other side of the pit, Vex was sitting on the floor of the chamber, breathing hard, staring at his hands. One stone. One in a glove.
He looked at them for a long time.
Then he looked at me.
"Thank you," he said finally.
Very quietly. So quietly I barely heard it. As if the words hurt to say. As if he'd never said them before in his whole life, and didn't know if he was doing it right.
Vera sat down on the floor next to her brother. She didn't say anything. She just put her arm around him.
And he let her.
He put his head on his sister's shoulder, and closed his eyes, and his shoulders started to shake, and he didn't make a sound.
"The Key," said Ela, after a while. Very gently. "Kuzey. The Key. Before he comes."
I looked up at the ceiling. At the bronze needle, glowing green among its stone feathers, high above the pit.
I couldn't stand up. My legs wouldn't work. So I lay there on my back, and I reached up toward it. Not with my hand. With the wind.
*Poyraz,* I called. *Northeast wind. Wind of the Black Sea. Wind of my city. Please.*
The whole chamber started to shake.
The tiny stone figures on the floor rattled. The beads rolled. Dust poured from the ceiling. Uncle Tarık grabbed Ela and pulled her back from the edge. Bora grabbed Vex and Vera.
And out of the pit came a wind.

A great wind. Round and spinning. Rising up out of the darkness like the breath of something enormous. Warm and wet and smelling of rain, of the first rain after a long dry summer, of green leaves and wet earth and flowers opening.
And from the deep darkness, riding on the wind, something rose.
A serpent.

It was as long as a train. Its body coiled up out of the pit, around and around, filling the chamber, its scales shining green and gold in the light of the flashlight. Huge scales, each one as big as my hand, overlapping like the tiles on a roof, rippling as it moved.

And around its head grew a great ring of feathers. Long, curving feathers, bright green, the green of a quetzal bird, the most beautiful bird in the world, shimmering blue and gold when the light caught them. They rippled and moved in the wind that came off the serpent's own body, like a lion's mane in a breeze.

Its head was huge. Bigger than a car. Its eyes were gold and very, very old. Older than the city of the gods. Older than the pyramids. Older than anything I had ever seen. Wise and calm and a little sad.
When it breathed, the air in the chamber spun in slow circles around us, lifting our hair, rustling the feathers carved on the ceiling.
*The Feathered Serpent,* whispered the hot Mexican wind, in awe. It had stopped chattering. For the first time, it was silent. *Ehecatl. The wind that sweeps the road for the rain.*
The serpent looked at me. Lying on the floor, with my arm hanging uselessly.
Then at Vex. Sitting against the wall, with his sister's arm around him, his face wet.
Then back at me.
When it spoke, its voice sounded like wind blowing through a thousand reed flutes. Soft and hollow and musical. It filled the whole chamber. It filled my whole head.
*I saw what you did, Windborn.*
I didn't know what to say.
*You fell for your enemy. You jumped into the dark. You caught him.*
"I didn't really think about it," I said. "I just did it."

*Yes,* said the Feathered Serpent. *That is the point. The ones who think about it first, who weigh it, who decide if the enemy is worth saving... they are good people. But the ones who simply jump...* The great golden eyes blinked, very slowly. *They are rare.*
It lowered its huge feathered head until its eye was right in front of my face. So close that I could see myself reflected in it. A small, dirty, scared boy, lying on a stone floor.

*Long ago,* said the serpent, *before this world, there was another world. And it ended. And all its people were gone. Only their bones were left, deep in the land of the dead. Mictlan. Nine levels down. And I went down there. All the way down. Through the rivers and the mountains and the winds made of knives. I went down into the dark to bring back the bones of the old world, so that the new people could be made. So that you could live.*
The feathers rippled.
*It was very dark. And very cold. And I was very afraid. But I went down. For someone else.*
The great eye blinked again.
*I know what it costs to go down into the dark for someone else, Windborn. I know.*

chapters.t: Chapter Nineteen: The Gift of the Serpent
p: The Feathered Serpent lifted its head.
*You do not need a test,* it said. *You have passed it already. You passed it when you jumped.*
It breathed out.

A long, warm, spiraling wind. Smelling of rain. It rose up through the chamber, around and around, up to the ceiling, to the bronze needle among the stone feathers. And the needle came loose. Easily. As if it had only been waiting.
It floated down through the air. Slowly. Turning. Glowing green. Down, down, past the serpent's great feathered head, down to me.
Into my hand. My good hand.
It was warm. It felt alive. Like holding a bird. A small bird, with its heart beating very fast against your palm.
The Poyraz. The northeast wind. The great wind of the Black Sea. The fourth Key.
And it spoke.

Not like the others. The others spoke in my head. The Poyraz spoke in a voice I *knew.* It was the wind that blew down the Bosphorus every winter. The wind that rattled Grandma's windows. The wind that made the ferries rock and the seagulls give up flying and sit on the lamp posts, looking annoyed. The wind I had heard my whole life, without knowing it was talking to me.
*Kuzey,* it said. *Little Kuzey. From the fifth floor. With the ketchup on your börek.*
I laughed. Out loud. With tears running down my face.
"You know me?"

*I have known you since you were born,* said the Poyraz. *I was blowing on the night you were born. Your grandmother told you it was the north wind, howling like a happy wolf. It was not. It was me. I came down the Bosphorus to see you. I sang at your window.*
"Grandma said it was the Yıldız."
*Your grandmother,* said the Poyraz, *is wonderful, but she does not always get the details right.*
Inside me, I felt the Yıldız, the North Wind, huff, very offended. The Poyraz laughed.
"Four," whispered Ela. She was holding the Clue Book against her chest. "Four to two. Kuzey, it's four to two."
And from the doorway behind us, from the other side of the silver lake, a cold voice said:
"Not for long."
Mordecai Vane stepped into the chamber.
He hadn't used the stepping stones. He had frozen the lake. The whole lake of mercury, solid, from wall to wall, a sheet of silver ice. He had walked straight across it.

Frost spread across the floor of the chamber with every step he took. The little green statues turned white. The beads froze to the stone. Behind him, across the frozen silver lake, came Grays. More than I could count. Their fog-gray eyes glowing in the dark. Some of them had bee stings all over their faces.
The Feathered Serpent hissed.

It was the loudest sound I had ever heard. Like a thousand flutes all screaming at once. Its feathers flared out around its head, huge and green and blazing. And a blast of hot, wet wind roared out of it, straight at Mordecai. A wind that could have knocked down a house.
Mordecai raised his stone hand.
The wind froze in midair.
It turned into a wall of glittering ice. Right there. In the air. Thousands of tiny ice crystals, hanging, frozen, sparkling. Then it fell. And shattered on the floor into a thousand pieces.
"Hello, old snake," said Mordecai. "I'll deal with you later."
He looked terrible.

Worse than on Mount Fuji. Much worse. His face was gray and thin and covered in sweat, even in the cold. He was breathing hard, in short, shallow breaths. His stone hand was cracked all the way up to his elbow now, and it was shaking. Little pieces of stone kept falling off it. In his fist, the two Keys, the Lodos and the Gündoğusu, were screaming so loudly that even Uncle Tarık could hear them. Two thin, high, endless screams.
But his eyes were the same. Cold and green and hard.
He looked at me, lying on the floor with the Poyraz in my hand. He looked at the Feathered Serpent. He looked at his son, sitting against the wall with his sister's arm around him.
Then he turned his stone hand toward Uncle Tarık.
"No!" I yelled.
Too late.

White mist shot from Mordecai's fingers. Ice crawled up Uncle Tarık's legs. Fast. Much faster than in Crete. Up his legs, over his knees, up his body, over his chest, his arms, his shoulders. And stopped at his neck.
He stood there, frozen. A statue of ice, with only his head free. His eyes wide. His breath coming out in little white clouds. His glasses frosted over.
"DAD!" screamed Ela.

"It's quite simple, Kuzey," said Mordecai. His voice was perfectly calm. "Last time, in Crete, the ice stopped at his chest. This time I will not stop. In one minute, it will cover his head. In two, he will be a statue." He held out his gray hand. "Give me the Poyraz."
I looked at the Key in my hand.
It was warm. Alive. The wind of my city. The wind that had sung at my window on the night I was born.
*Don't,* whispered the Poyraz. *Don't, little Kuzey.*
Then I looked at Uncle Tarık.

Funny, clumsy Uncle Tarık. Who used all his airline miles for us. Who always got lost. Who held his flashlight upside down. Who stood in front of six Grays with an umbrella. Who flew a kite on the Kamo River. Who had never complained once, not on any of our trips, not in Iceland or Egypt or Japan, not about the toilets or the cold or the trolls.
Whose lips were turning blue.
The ice was creeping up his neck. Over his chin. Toward his mouth.
"Don't, Kuzey!" he gasped. "Don't you *dare!* The Keys are more important than me! Your grandmother... the whole world... don't!"
"No," I said. "They're not."
I didn't even have to think about it. Not really. It was like the pit. I just knew.
"I'm sorry," I whispered to the Poyraz. "I'm so sorry. I'll come and get you. I promise. I'll get you back. All of you."
*I know,* said the Poyraz. Very quietly. *I know you will.*
I threw the Poyraz Key across the chamber.
Mordecai caught it in his gray hand. And smiled.
The Poyraz screamed. I heard it. I felt it. Like a knife in my chest. A third scream, joining the other two, high and thin and terrible.

Mordecai snapped the fingers of his human hand. The ice around Uncle Tarık cracked. And fell away. All at once. Into a pile of white shards on the floor. And Uncle Tarık collapsed onto his knees, gasping, shaking, his lips blue, his skin white.
Ela threw herself on him, sobbing. She wrapped her arms around him and held on as tight as she could, and he held her back, and they knelt there on the floor of the chamber together, shaking.
"Three to three," said Mordecai, tucking the Key into his coat, with the other two.
He coughed. A long, rattling cough. His stone hand shook so much that more pieces fell off it. He had to lean against the wall.
But he was still smiling.
"Thank you, Kuzey," he said, when he could speak again. "You're just like your grandmother. Soft. Always soft." He straightened up. "That's why you'll lose."
He turned to go. Then he stopped.
He looked at his children.
At Vera, sitting on the floor with her arm around her brother.
At Vex.
"Vex," he said. "Come."
Vex stood up slowly.
He was shaking. His face was still wet. His stone hand hung at his side, gray and cracked. His other hand, in its glove, was clenched into a fist.
He looked at his father.
He looked at Vera.
He looked at me, lying on the floor with my arm hanging uselessly, where I had fallen after pulling him out of the dark.

The chamber was completely silent. The Grays stood in the doorway, waiting, their fog eyes glowing. The Feathered Serpent was very still, its great golden eyes moving from father to son. Even the screaming Keys in Mordecai's fist seemed to go quiet. As if they were listening too.
"No," said Vex.
It came out very small. Like a whisper. Like the first crack in a frozen lake.
Mordecai went very still.
"Excuse me?" he said softly.
Vex swallowed. His hands were shaking. But his voice, when it came again, wasn't.
"You heard me," he said. "No."
He took a breath.

"I fell into a pit today, Dad," he said. "A pit. In the dark. I was going to die. I *was.* And he jumped in after me." He pointed at me. With his stone hand. "He jumped into the dark. After me. After everything I did to him." His voice cracked. "And you didn't even notice I was gone. You walked in here, and you looked at the Key, and you looked at the snake, and you looked at the professor. You didn't even *ask.*"
For a moment, something moved on Mordecai's face.
Something that looked almost like pain. Like someone had pressed on an old bruise.
His mouth opened. As if he was going to say something. As if he was going to ask, *Are you hurt?*
Then it was gone. Frozen over. Like a lake in winter.
"You will regret this," he said. Very quietly. "Both of you."
"Maybe," said Vera, standing up next to her brother. She took his hand. His stone hand. She held it in both of hers, without flinching. "But not as much as you will."
Mordecai looked at them. His two children. Standing together, side by side, holding hands, the way they had when they were small, on a beach, on a Sunday, flying kites.
He looked at them for a long, long moment.
Then he turned and walked out of the chamber. Across the frozen silver lake. His Grays behind him, in a line. The frost following him like a cold shadow.
He didn't look back.
When he was gone, the chamber was very quiet.

The frost slowly melted from the little green statues. The beads unfroze from the floor. Across the doorway, we could hear the silver lake cracking and groaning as the ice melted, turning back into heavy, shining liquid.
The Feathered Serpent breathed out slowly. A long, sad, warm breath. Its feathers drooped around its head, like a flower closing.
*He is very lonely, that one,* it said.
Nobody answered.

*Lonely people,* said the Feathered Serpent, *build cold houses. They make the walls thick and the windows small and the fires low. They tell themselves it is to keep the bad things out.* The great golden eyes looked at the doorway where Mordecai had gone. *But it keeps everything out. The good things too. Until there is no one left inside but themselves. And it is very, very cold.*
Vex sat down hard on the floor.
He looked like he might cry. And also like he might punch the next person who noticed.
Nobody noticed. Very carefully. Ela looked at the Clue Book. Uncle Tarık looked at his frozen glasses, wiping them on his shirt. Vera looked at the ceiling.
Bora, who notices everything, went over and sat down next to him.

He reached into his pocket. And he took something out. A plastic bag, a bit squashed. Inside it was a slice of mango, covered in red chili powder. The last one. From the man at the side of the road on the Avenue of the Dead. He had bought it on the way in, when Ela wasn't looking.
He handed it to Vex.
"Emergency," he explained.
Vex stared at it. Then at Bora.
"You're giving me your mango," he said slowly. "After everything."
"It's the last one," said Bora. "And you look like you need it more than me. And that's saying something, because I *really* need it. I've been thinking about it for two hours."
Vex looked at the mango for a long time.

Then, for the first time since I met him, on the stairs of Grandma's building, a lifetime ago, he laughed. A rough, surprised, cracked laugh. Like he'd forgotten how. Like a door that hasn't been opened for years, creaking.
He ate the mango.
He made a face. The chili was very hot. His eyes watered. His nose ran.
"That," he said, coughing, "is disgusting."
"I know," said Bora happily. "Isn't it great?"
Vex laughed again.
The Feathered Serpent came to me, last of all.

It lowered its head until its great golden eye was right in front of me again. I was sitting up now, against the wall, holding my bad arm. Uncle Tarık had made a sling for it out of Grandma's scarf, very carefully, so it wouldn't get dirty.
*Your arm,* said the serpent.
"It's okay," I said. "It just hurts."
The serpent breathed on it.

A warm, wet breath, smelling of rain and earth and growing things. It wrapped around my arm and my shoulder, gently, like a bandage made of air. And the pain went away. Not all at once. Slowly. Like ice melting. Until I could move my fingers. Then my wrist. Then my elbow.
"Thank you," I whispered.

*I cannot fix the boy's hand,* said the Feathered Serpent, looking at Vex. *I am sorry. The cold is too deep. Only the one who put it there can take it away. Or the winds themselves, when they are free.*
Vex looked down at his stone hand, and didn't say anything.

*And I cannot follow you to the Gate,* said the serpent. *My place is here. Under the city of the gods. Sweeping the road for the rain.* The golden eyes blinked. *But I will be listening, Windborn. On the day the Gate opens, every wind in the world will be listening. And so will I.*
It rose up. Its great green-and-gold body uncoiled, around and around, back toward the pit.
*Remember what you promised the Black Wind,* it said. *In the ice. Remember what you are.*
"What am I?" I said.
The Feathered Serpent looked down at me one last time.
*The one who asks,* it said.
Then it sank down into the pit, into the darkness, its feathers glowing green, down and down, until there was only a faint green light, far below. And then not even that.
Just the breathing. Warm and slow. In and out.
And then that faded too.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Five: Rain on the City of the Gods
p: When we climbed out of the hole at the foot of the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, it was raining.
In December. In the dry season. Out of a sky that had been completely blue that morning.

Soft, warm rain. Falling gently on the courtyard, on the hundred stone heads of the temple, on the long Avenue of the Dead, on the Pyramid of the Sun. The stones turned dark and shiny. The dust turned to mud. The cactus plants in the cracks of the walls glistened. And the air smelled wonderful. Like wet earth and stone and green things, all at once.
"Ehecatl," said Uncle Tarık softly, standing in the rain with his face turned up. "The wind that sweeps the road for the rain. He swept it. Look."
The iguana was still lying by the ladder, where Bora had left him. He had his eyes closed and his mouth open, and his head tipped back, catching the raindrops on his tongue.
"He says," said Bora, crouching down next to him, "that this is the best day of his life. He says it hasn't rained here in December since he was an egg."
"Tell him thank you," I said. "For guarding the entrance."
Bora told him. The iguana opened one eye, looked at me for a long moment, then closed it again.
"He says," said Bora, "you're welcome. He says he was very good at it. He says nobody came in at all, except the cold man, and he didn't count, because the iguana was asleep."
Vex laughed. A short, surprised laugh. Then he looked embarrassed and stopped.
We walked back down the Avenue of the Dead in the rain. Slowly. All of us soaked. Nobody minded.

The Grays were still out there. We could see them in the distance, on the platforms beside the road, wandering in circles, waving at the last few bees. One of them was sitting on the ground with his hat in his hands, looking up at the rain, as if he had never seen rain before. As if he was trying to remember something.
"They look lost," said Vera quietly.

"They are lost," said Vex. "They don't know who they are. Not really. Father took that away." He looked at his own stone hand, wet with rain. "I used to think they were just... things. Like furniture. I never thought about it." He was quiet. "They were people once. Somebody's dad. Somebody's brother."
Nobody said anything.

At the end of the avenue, where the road met the car park, there was an old woman selling clay whistles shaped like birds, under a plastic sheet. She was the only person there. When she saw us coming, soaked, out of the rain, she held one up.
Bora bought six. One for each of us.
We walked to the car blowing them. They sounded like birds singing in the rain.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Six: Meanwhile, on the Fog Road
p: *Kuzey never saw this. Nobody did. Not even Vex. But the winds saw. The winds see everything. And one day, much later, the Lodos told him.*
Halfway along the fog road, between Mexico and Turkey, in the middle of the cold gray nothing, Mordecai Vane stopped walking.
The Grays stopped too. Behind him. In a line. They didn't ask why. Grays never ask.
He stood there in the fog. For a long time.
Then he sat down.

There was no ground on the fog road. There was nothing to sit on. But he sat anyway, in the gray, with his knees pulled up, like a boy. His stone hand rested on his knee, with the three Keys in it. The Lodos, cold and gray. The Gündoğusu, fading. And the Poyraz, newest of all, still glowing green, fighting him, fighting him, every second.
All three of them were screaming.
He listened to them scream for a long time.

He remembered a beach. In Cornwall. On a Sunday. Wind coming off the sea, cold and salty. Two small children, a boy and a girl, with pale hair, running along the sand, holding a kite string between them, laughing, shouting, *Dad! Dad, look! Look how high!*
He remembered his wife. Sitting on a blanket on the sand, with a flask of tea. Watching them. Watching him. Smiling.
*You're good at this,* she had said. *You know exactly how to hold the string.*
*I know how the wind works,* he had said. *I've read every book.*
*No,* she had said, laughing. *You don't hold it like a man who's read a book. You hold it like a man who loves it.*
He sat in the fog with his stone hand on his knee.
Then he took off his gray glove, the one on his human hand, the left one. He hadn't taken it off in years. He looked at his hand. Pale. Thin. Real.
He held it up. Into the fog. Fingers spread. The way you'd hold your hand out of a car window, to feel the wind.
There was no wind on the fog road. There never was.
He held it there anyway. For a long, long time.
Then he put the glove back on. And stood up. And walked on, toward Turkey, toward the Gate, without looking back.
But the Lodos, screaming in his fist, had seen.
And for the first time since Crete, it stopped screaming. Just for a moment.
And it wondered.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Seven: Meanwhile, Beside the Gate
p: *Grandma Nermin told Kuzey about this, much later. She told it while she was making tea.*
He came down the eighteen floors of Derinkuyu very slowly. Much more slowly than before. Leaning on the walls. Stopping on every landing to rest. Coughing.
When he came into the little stone room beside the Gate, Grandma Nermin looked up from her knitting.
She looked at him for a long time.
