At his gray face. At the sweat on his forehead. At the cracks running all the way up his stone arm now, past his elbow, onto his shoulder. At the three Keys in his fist, screaming so loudly that even she could hear them, without being a Windborn.
At his son, who was not with him.
"Where's Vex?" she said.
Mordecai didn't answer. He sat down, very heavily, in the chair across the little table from her. He put his stone hand on the table, with the Keys in it. It made a sound like a rock being dropped.
Grandma put down her knitting.

She got up. She went to the little stove in the corner. She filled the teapot from the jug of water. She lit the stove. And she waited, without saying anything, until the water boiled, and the teapot started to sing.
She made two glasses of tea. Strong, and dark red, the way it's made in Turkey, in little tulip-shaped glasses. She put one in front of him. With two sugar cubes on the saucer.
He looked at it.
"Two sugars," he said.
"You always took two sugars," said Grandma. "On Tuesdays. Forty years ago. In my kitchen. I remember."
Mordecai looked at the tea for a long time. Steam was rising from it, curling up into the cold air of the underground room.
Then, very slowly, with his human hand, he picked it up. He put the two sugars in. He stirred it, with the little spoon, *clink, clink, clink,* the way Turkish people do. And he drank it.
Neither of them said anything.
Outside the little room, the Gate of Seven Winds hummed. Seven colors flickered through the cracks around it.
"He chose them," said Mordecai at last. To his tea. "Vex. He chose them. Over me. Both of them did."
"I know," said Grandma. "The wind told me."
"The boy jumped into a pit to save him." Mordecai's voice was strange. "A pit. In the dark. He jumped in. After everything Vex did."
"That's my grandson," said Grandma.
Mordecai put down his glass.
"I didn't notice he was gone," he said. Very quietly. "Vex. He fell. And I didn't notice. I walked into the room, and I looked at the Key, and I didn't..." He stopped.
Grandma Nermin reached across the table. She put her old, wrinkled hand on top of his human hand. His left one. The one that was still real.
He didn't pull away.

"Mordecai," she said gently. "You're not cold. You're sad. You've been sad for a very, very long time. Since Elizabeth died. And you've been trying not to feel it. That's what the hand is for, isn't it? That's what it's always been for. Not the winds. So you don't have to feel anything."
He didn't say anything.
He didn't move his hand.

They sat like that for a long time, in the little stone room, at the bottom of the world, beside the Gate. The old teacher and her old student. With two empty tea glasses between them, and three screaming winds.
Then he stood up. Very suddenly. And pulled his hand away. And walked to the door.
"The boy will come," he said, without turning around. "In a few days. With his Keys. And then it will all be over."
"Yes," said Grandma Nermin. "I think it will."
He went out.
She sat there for a while, looking at his empty glass.

Then she picked up her knitting again. The scarf was almost finished. It was blue, with little white flowers. Exactly like the one she had been wearing on the day she was taken. The one she had left behind, in the kitchen, on the hook by the door.
She was knitting it for someone. She hadn't decided who yet.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Pyramid of the Moon
p: That night, we sat on top of the Pyramid of the Moon, looking down at the Avenue of the Dead in the moonlight.

We weren't supposed to be up there. The pyramids close at five o'clock. But I flew everyone up. One at a time. Very carefully. Even Bora. He kept his eyes shut the whole way and said "I'm fine I'm fine I'm fine" and then sat down in the very middle of the flat top, as far from the edge as possible, and didn't move.

Rodrigo had driven back to Mexico City to fetch Don Tomás and some food. He came back with enough tacos for twenty people and a thermos of hot chocolate with cinnamon and chili in it. Don Tomás came too. He stood at the bottom of the pyramid and shouted up at us, and refused to be flown up, and said he was "too old to become a bird now."
So we ate tacos on top of the Pyramid of the Moon, and drank the hot chocolate, and looked down at the city of the gods.

In the moonlight, it was silver and black. The long straight avenue ran away from us into the distance. The Pyramid of the Sun rose up on the left, huge and dark. And at the far end, at the very end, was the courtyard of the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, where it had all happened. Where I had jumped.

Uncle Tarık was wrapped in three blankets. He was still cold, deep down, even though the Feathered Serpent had breathed on him too. Ela hadn't let go of his arm for five hours. She was holding it now, with her head on his shoulder.
"I'm sorry," I said to everyone. "I gave him the Key. Now it's three to three."

"You saved my dad," said Ela fiercely, without lifting her head. "Don't you *ever* say sorry for that. Ever. I'll put it in the Clue Book. On the first page. *Kuzey is not allowed to say sorry for saving Dad.*"
"And the Keys he has are trying to come back to you," said Bora, with his mouth full of taco. "Fūjin said so. Every second, they're fighting him."
"He looked sick," said Vera quietly. "Didn't he? Really sick."
Nobody said anything.
Vex and Vera were sitting a little apart from us, at the edge of the flat top. Side by side. Vex had his knees pulled up. Vera had a blanket around both of them.
Then Vex cleared his throat.
"I know where your grandmother is," he said.
Everyone turned.

"Exactly where," said Vex. "I've been there. He made me bring her food. In the tower. And now." He looked at his hands. "She was nice to me. Even then. Even after... everything. She asked about my school. She asked what I wanted to be when I grew up." His voice went rough. "Nobody ever asked me that."
"What did you say?" asked Ela softly.
Vex was quiet for a long time.
"I said I didn't know," he said. "I said I'd never thought about it. Because I always thought I'd just be... him."
He looked out at the moonlit city.
"She said, 'Well, you've got plenty of time to think about it. And you don't have to be anybody but yourself.'" He shook his head. "I didn't understand what she meant. I think I do now."
"Where is she, Vex?" I said. My heart was pounding. "Exactly?"
He turned to look at me.

"Cappadocia," he said. "Under the ground. In the underground city. Derinkuyu. Eighteen floors deep. People hid there from wars, thousands of years ago. Thousands of people." He took a breath. "At the very bottom, there's a door. With seven sides. And seven holes. The Gate of Seven Winds. She's in a little room right next to it. With a teapot."
"A teapot?" I said.
"He gave her a teapot," said Vex. "I don't know why."
I did. I knew exactly why. *A kitchen without boiling tea is just a room with a fridge in it.*

"He's keeping her there because she's the Keeper," said Vex. "Only the Keeper's blood can wake the Gate. That's what the old book says. A drop of the Keeper's blood, and all seven Keys. And then it opens."
I took out the leather map. I unrolled it on the stone top of the Pyramid of the Moon, in the moonlight. Ela held one end. Bora held the other.
Six stars were dark now.
Only one star was left. In the very center of Turkey. Glowing brighter than ever. Pulsing like a heartbeat. Fast. Faster than before.
"The Kıble," said Ela softly. "The south wind. The seventh Key. It's at the Gate too. It must be."
"So whoever gets there first," said Vex, "wins everything."
On top of the Pyramid of the Moon, after the tacos, Ela went and sat down in front of Vex.
Just sat down. Cross-legged. Right in front of him. With the Clue Book open on her knees and her pencil in her hand.
Vex looked at her warily.
"What?" he said.
"I have some questions," said Ela.
"Ela," said Vera, warningly.
"It's okay," said Vex. He looked at Ela. "Go on, then. Ask."
Ela pushed her glasses up her nose.
"Question one," she said. "In Athens. At the Tower of the Winds. You told the Grays to take Kuzey. If they'd taken him, what would your father have done?"
Vex was quiet for a moment. "Made him find the Keys," he said. "Then taken them out of him. With the hand."
"Would it have hurt him?"
"Yes."
Ela wrote that down.
"Question two. In Crete. You froze my dad. Up to his chest. Would you have frozen him all the way? If Kuzey hadn't given you the Key?"
Vex looked at Uncle Tarık. Uncle Tarık looked back at him, from inside his three blankets.
"I don't know," said Vex. Very quietly. "I don't think so. I think I would have stopped. I hope I would have stopped." He swallowed. "I don't know."
Ela wrote that down too.
"Question three. In Egypt. You grabbed me. You put frost on my shoulder. It hurt for two days. Why?"
"Because I was scared," said Vex. "Because Father said if I failed again..." He stopped. "Because I was scared."
"Of what?"
Vex looked at his stone hand.

"Of this," he said. "Of becoming this. All the way. And of him. Of what his face looks like when I fail." He looked up at her. "Do you want to know what it looks like? It doesn't look like anything. That's the worst part. It just goes blank. Like I'm not there anymore."
Ela didn't write that down. She just looked at him.
"Question four," she said. "The last one." She closed the Clue Book. "Are you sorry?"
The top of the pyramid was very quiet. The wind blew across it, hot and dry, rustling the blankets.
Vex didn't answer for a long, long time.

"Yes," he said finally. "I'm sorry. I'm sorry about Athens. And Crete. And your dad. And your shoulder. I'm sorry about all of it." His voice was very rough. "I don't know if that's enough. I don't think it's enough. But I'm sorry."
Ela looked at him for a long time.
Then she opened the Clue Book again. She turned to a new page. And at the top, she wrote:
*VEX VANE*
And under it:
*Trust: 10%*
She showed it to him.
Vex looked at it. Then he almost smiled.
"Ten percent," he said.
"It's a start," said Ela. "Vera started at zero. She's at ninety-five now." She closed the book and stood up. "Don't mess it up."
"I won't," said Vex.
"I'll be watching," said Ela.
"I know," said Vex. "Vera told me. You watch everything."
Ela almost smiled too. Then she went back and sat down next to her dad.
Later, much later, when everyone else was asleep on top of the pyramid, wrapped in blankets, I woke up and saw Vex and Vera still sitting at the edge. Talking very quietly.
I didn't mean to listen. But the wind was blowing toward me, and the wind carries everything.
"Does it hurt?" Vera was asking. "Your hand?"
"All the time," said Vex. "Like holding ice. Forever." He was quiet. "Father said it stops hurting. After a while. He said you stop feeling it."
"Did it stop for him?"
Vex didn't answer for a long time.
"No," he said. "I don't think it ever stopped for him. I think he just stopped saying it hurt."
Vera took his stone hand in both of hers again. The way she had in the chamber. She held it in her lap, in the moonlight.
"Do you remember Mom's compass?" she said. "The one she gave you? When she gave me the bracelet?"
Vex went very still.
"I lost it," he said.
"I know," said Vera. "You cried for a week."
"I didn't."
"You did. I heard you. Every night. Under your blanket."
Vex didn't say anything.
"I found it," said Vera.
He turned to stare at her.

"In Father's desk," she said. "Last year. In a drawer. With some papers. He must have found it, and kept it." She reached into her pocket. And she took out something small and round and silver, and held it out to him in the moonlight.
A little silver compass. Old. Scratched. With a cracked glass face.
Vex stared at it.

"I was going to give it back to you," said Vera. "For a whole year, I was going to. But I was scared you'd give it to him. Or tell him I took it." She pressed it into his hand. His human hand, the one in the glove. "I'm not scared anymore."
Vex looked at the compass for a long time.
The needle was swinging. Around and around. Not pointing north. Not pointing anywhere.
Then, slowly, it stopped. And pointed.
Not north.
At me.
Asleep, or pretending to be asleep, ten meters away, in a blanket, on top of the Pyramid of the Moon.
"It's one of those," said Vex, very quietly. "Isn't it? Like the old man's in the bazaar. Kaptan Murat's. It points to the nearest Key. Or the nearest Windborn."
"Mom was in the Order," said Vera. "Did you know that?"
"No," said Vex.

"Neither did I," said Vera. "Until Grandma Nermin told me. In the tower. She said Mom was a Keeper's daughter. From Cornwall. She said Mom gave up the Order when she married Father. Because she loved him."
The twins sat there for a long time in silence, looking at the little compass.
"She'd hate this," said Vex finally. "Wouldn't she? All of it. What he's doing. What I did."
"Yes," said Vera.
"Then I'm going to stop it," said Vex.
Before we left Mexico, Vera kept her promise.

"Shoes," she said, the morning after the pyramid, back in the city, at breakfast in the hotel, pointing at Bora's feet. He was wearing one shoe and one of Uncle Tarık's socks, with a plastic bag tied over it. "I said I'd buy you new shoes. Better ones."
So we went to the market.

Not a shop. A market. The biggest one any of us had ever seen. La Merced, it was called. It was like the Grand Bazaar and the Khan el-Khalili and every market in the world, all squashed together and made even bigger and louder and more colorful. Piles of chili peppers in every color: red and green and orange and black and brown, big and small, fresh and dried, in mountains as tall as Bora. Pyramids of oranges and mangoes and papayas and fruits I had never seen before, purple and spiky and strange. Flowers everywhere. Sweets everywhere. Toys and piñatas and clothes and pots and pans and statues of saints and cages full of chickens.
And masks.

A whole street of masks. Wrestling masks. Bright, shiny masks, made of stretchy material, in every color, with patterns of flames and stars and lightning and skulls. They're for lucha libre, Vera explained. Mexican wrestling. The wrestlers wear masks, and nobody ever knows who they really are. Not even their friends. Not even their families. They wear them their whole lives.
Bora stopped in the middle of the street and stared at them with his mouth open.
"I need one," he said.
"You need *shoes,*" said Vera.
"I need one," said Bora, "*and* shoes."
So Vera bought him both.

The shoes were bright red sneakers, with white soles and a picture of a lightning bolt on the side. They were the brightest shoes I had ever seen. Bora loved them so much that he wore them out of the shop and kept looking down at his feet as he walked, and walked into a stall full of piñatas, and had to apologize to all of them.
The mask was gold. Shiny gold, with black around the eyes, and red flames up the sides, and a silver star on the forehead. Bora put it on immediately.
"I am," he said, in a deep voice, from inside the mask, "EL GRAN BORA."
"Oh no," said Ela.
"EL GRAN BORA," said Bora, "FEARS NOTHING."
"Except the dark," said Ela. "And heights. And running out of food."
"EL GRAN BORA," said Bora, with great dignity, "FEARS ONLY THREE THINGS."
Vera was laughing so hard she had to sit down on a box of mangoes.

Then she bought masks for all of us. A blue one with silver stars for Ela. A black one with white lightning for me. A green one with gold feathers for Uncle Tarık, which he wore on his head like a hat.
And one for Vex. Plain silver, with no pattern at all. She gave it to him without saying anything.
Vex held it for a long time. Then he put it on.
He looked at himself in a little mirror at the side of the stall. Just his eyes, through the holes in the silver mask. Green eyes. His mother's eyes, Don Tomás had said.
"Nobody knows who you really are," he said slowly. "Under a mask. You can be anybody."
"Or you can take it off," said Vera, "and be yourself."
Vex looked at her in the mirror.
Then he took off the mask, and looked at his own face for a long time.
He kept the mask, though. He put it in his pocket, next to the little silver compass.
That last night in Mexico City, on the hotel roof, I tried to practice. And I couldn't.
It felt wrong. All of it. The three winds inside me were there, the North and the Black and the Keşişleme, but they were quiet. Sad. Like three people at a table where a fourth chair is empty.
The Poyraz. The wind of my city. I'd held it for about five minutes. Five minutes. And then I'd thrown it away.
And now it was in Mordecai's fist. With the Lodos and the Gündoğusu. Screaming.

I stood on the roof and looked out at the lights of Mexico City, spreading away in every direction, to the dark mountains, and I tried to make a rainbow. Like on Dr. Amira's roof in Cairo. Something nice. Something to cheer us up.
Nothing happened.
*We're sorry, Windborn,* said the North Wind. *We are thinking about our brother. We cannot make beautiful things tonight.*
*The Poyraz,* said the Black Wind, *was always the loudest of us. The bossiest. The one who blew the ferries around.* It paused. *It is very quiet without him.*
The Keşişleme didn't say anything at all. That was the worst part. The Keşişleme always said something.
I sat down on the edge of the roof.
After a while, someone sat down next to me.
It was Vex. He had his little silver compass in his gloved hand. The needle was pointing at me.
He didn't say anything for a long time. We just sat there, looking at the city.
"I could hear them," he said finally. "When I was with him. The Keys. In his hand. Screaming." He looked at the compass. "I used to put my fingers in my ears at night. In the tower. It didn't help."
"I can hear them now," I said. "Even from here. Very faint. Three of them."

"He'll be at the Gate by now," said Vex. "Holding them. Waiting." He turned the compass over in his fingers. "He's dying, you know. I think he's dying. The hand is killing him. Every Key he holds makes it worse. The cracks are on his shoulder now. I saw them. When it reaches his heart..." He stopped.
I didn't say anything.
"I hate him," said Vex. "For what he did. To your grandmother. To you. To Vera. To me." He held up his stone hand. "For this. I hate him so much."
He was quiet.
"And I don't want him to die," he said. Very, very quietly. "Isn't that stupid?"
"No," I said. "That's not stupid. That's just... how it is. When it's your family."
We sat there for a long time.
Then I said, "Vex. When we get to the Gate. Will you help me?"
He looked at me, surprised.
"Help you do what?"
I looked out at the city. At the mountains. At the two volcanoes, the warrior and the princess, dark against the stars, with a thin plume of smoke rising from the warrior's torch.
"I don't know yet," I said. "Not exactly. But I think... I think I'm going to need someone who knows him. Who knows how he thinks. Someone who knows what he's afraid of."
Vex looked at the compass in his hand for a long time.

"He's afraid of being outside," he said slowly. "Outside the house. In the cold. Looking in the window." He looked at me. "That's what he always says. When he talks about the winds. That's the thing he's most afraid of."
"I know," I said. "He told me. In the northern lights."
Vex stared at me.
Then he slowly nodded.
"I'll help," he said.
And somewhere inside me, very faintly, for the first time since the chamber under the temple, the Keşişleme said something.
*Hm,* it said. *Interesting.*

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-Three: The Kites Are Still Flying
p: On our last morning in Mexico, we went back to Teotihuacan one more time, to say goodbye to Don Tomás.

He was waiting for us at the bottom of the Pyramid of the Moon, where he had made Rodrigo bring him, sitting on a stone, with his big straw hat on, and Rodrigo standing next to him with the car. The sun was coming up over the mountains, pink and gold. The city of the gods was waking up. Somewhere, a rooster was crowing. A man was setting up a stall at the side of the avenue, selling little clay whistles shaped like birds.
Don Tomás stood up when he saw us coming down. Slowly. Leaning on Rodrigo.
He looked at all of us. At Uncle Tarık in his blankets. At Ela with the Clue Book. At Bora with one shoe. At Vera.
And at Vex.
He looked at Vex for a long time. At his stone hand. At his face.
Then he took off his hat, and held it against his chest, the way he had when he first saw me.
"Welcome," he said to Vex. "Welcome to the Order of the Compass Rose."
Vex stared at him. "I'm not..."
"Your mother was," said Don Tomás. "Elizabeth. From Cornwall. A very good kite flyer. I met her once. Forty years ago. With Nermin." He smiled his wrinkled smile. "You have her eyes."
Vex didn't say anything. He couldn't.
Don Tomás turned to me.

"I am too old to come to Turkey," he said. "My legs are made of paper now. Like my kites." He held out his hand. In it was a roll of string. Very old. On a wooden spool. "But take this. It is the string from Nermin's kite. The serpent with seven tails. It is very strong. Stronger than it looks. She made it herself, from the hair of a horse from the Black Sea." He pressed it into my hand. "Use it. When you need to hold on to something."
"Thank you," I said.
He hugged me. A dry, bony, papery hug.
"Tell her," he whispered. "Tell Nermin. The kites are still flying."
We flew home that afternoon. To Turkey. To Istanbul.
Vera paid for the tickets with her father's card. Six tickets this time. Not five.
"He'll see this," said Vex, watching her hand the card over. "He'll see where we're going."
"Good," said Vera. "Let him."
The plane was huge. It flew across the whole of Mexico, then the Gulf, then the Atlantic Ocean, through the night. Thirteen hours. Nobody slept much.

Vex sat by the window. He hadn't been on a normal plane either, it turned out. He watched the clouds for hours, holding the little silver compass in his gloved hand. Every so often, he looked at it. The needle always pointed at me.
At one point, Bora leaned across the aisle and offered him a bag of peanuts.
Vex looked at the peanuts. Then at Bora.
"Why are you always giving me food?" he said.
"Because you always look hungry," said Bora.
Vex thought about this. Then he took the peanuts.
"Thank you," he said. It was getting easier for him to say it. You could hear.
"You're welcome," said Bora. "Next time, I'll give you a börek. My mom's. You'll cry. Everyone cries."
Somewhere over the Atlantic, in the dark, I took out the leather map one more time.
Six dark stars. One glowing.

And across the top of the map, in the empty space above the world, I noticed something I had never noticed before. Very faint. Written in ink so old and so pale that you could only see it at a certain angle, in a certain light.
Seven words. In Turkish. In handwriting I had seen on a hundred notes stuck to Grandma's fridge.
*The winds cannot be owned. Only borrowed.*
§CLUE Written very faintly across the top of the leather map, in Grandma's handwriting: The winds cannot be owned. Only borrowed.

I showed it to Ela. She stared at it for a long time. Then she opened the Clue Book to the very first page, where she had copied Grandma's letter, months ago, in Istanbul. And under it, Vera's mother's rule. And under that, *Kuzey is not allowed to say sorry for saving Dad.*
She wrote it again. Under all of them.
*The winds cannot be owned. Only borrowed.*
"I think," she said slowly, "that's the answer. To everything. I just don't know what the question is yet."
"Then we'll find out," I said. "At the Gate."
The plane flew on through the night. East. Toward the sunrise. Toward Turkey.
Toward home.
§END To be continued in Book Seven: The Gate of Seven Winds.

For hundreds of years, sailors on the Black Sea, the Bosphorus and the Mediterranean used a wind rose to name the winds. Each wind had its own name and its own personality, and every sailor knew them by heart. These are the seven winds of the Order of the Compass Rose.
**Yıldız (North).** Named after the North Star, *yıldız* means "star." A cold, clear, starry wind. Kuzey's own wind.
**Poyraz (Northeast).** The great wind of the Black Sea. When the Poyraz blows hard, the fishermen go home and the ferries rock.
**Gündoğusu (East).** "Sunrise." The wind that comes from where the sun is born each morning.
**Keşişleme (Southeast).** Named after the monks, the *keşiş,* who lived on the mountains to the southeast. A warm, dry wind from the deserts.
**Kıble (South).** The wind from the direction of Mecca. Hot, and full of sand.
**Lodos (Southwest).** A warm, wild, wet wind that brings big waves and headaches. People in Istanbul say the Lodos makes everyone grumpy.
**Karayel (Northwest).** "Black wind." A stormy, dark wind that brings clouds and sudden rain.
And the eighth, the west wind, the **Batı**, the one that would not make a deal? Nobody knows. It is still wild. That is another story.

chapters.t: The Real Places in This Book
p: **Tenochtitlan.** The Aztec capital really was built on an island in a lake, starting in the 1300s, where legend says an eagle sat on a cactus eating a snake. That eagle is on the flag of Mexico today. Mexico City really is built on the old lakebed, and parts of it really are sinking.
**Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl.** Two real volcanoes near Mexico City, with a real legend about a warrior and a princess. Popocatépetl really does smoke.

**Las Posadas.** For nine nights before Christmas, people in Mexico walk through the streets with candles, singing, asking for a place to stay, and end with food and a piñata. The traditional piñata really does have seven points.
**Xochimilco.** Real canals and floating gardens from Aztec times, with brightly painted boats called trajineras, and mariachis who play from boat to boat.
**Axolotls.** Real salamanders with feathery pink gills and permanent smiles. In the wild, they live almost nowhere except the canals of Xochimilco, and they are critically endangered.
**Coyoacán.** A real old neighborhood of Mexico City, with colorful houses and a fountain of two coyotes.

**Teotihuacan.** A real ancient city about 50 kilometers from Mexico City, built nearly 2,000 years ago by people whose name we don't even know. The Aztecs found it already in ruins and called it the place where the gods were born. It has the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon and the long Avenue of the Dead.

**The Temple of the Feathered Serpent.** Really covered in carved serpent heads with feathered collars. In 2003, archaeologists really did find a tunnel underneath it, more than 100 meters long, with walls sparkling with pyrite, thousands of offerings, three chambers at the end and pools of liquid mercury.

**Ehecatl.** The Aztec wind god, a form of Quetzalcoatl, who wore a mask with a long beak and swept the roads for the rain gods. In one old story, he really did go down to the underworld, Mictlan, to bring back the bones of the old world so new people could be made.
*Here is the first chapter of the next book,* The Gate of Seven Winds.
**Chapter One: Home**
The kettle in Grandma's kitchen was on the stove. Cold.
We stood in her flat in Kadıköy, the six of us, and nobody said anything.

I had left it boiling. On the day we went to the airport, all those weeks ago, I had filled it and lit the gas very low, so it would keep singing while we were gone. Mrs. Aksoy from downstairs must have turned it off. Of course she had. You can't leave a kettle on for two months. But I had hoped, somehow, stupidly, that it would still be singing when we got back.
It wasn't.

Everything else was exactly like the morning she disappeared. The teacups on the table. Her apron on its hook. The newspaper, open to the crossword, with half the answers filled in her neat handwriting. *Seven across: A wind from the north (6). POYRAZ.* The nine compasses on the shelf, where Ela and Bora and I had put them back, in the right order.
The smell of her. Cinnamon and old books.
Only the window was different. Somebody had fixed the glass that the storm had cracked, on the day it all began.
Outside, the ferries crossed the Bosphorus, and the seagulls screamed, and the city of Istanbul went on with its day, as if nothing in the world was wrong.

Paşa the cat came out from under the sofa. He looked at us. At me, and Ela, and Bora, and Uncle Tarık. Then at Vera and Vex, who were standing in the doorway, not sure if they were allowed to come in.
He walked straight past me. Straight past all of us. And went to Vex.
He sniffed Vex's shoes. He sniffed his stone hand, hanging at his side. Then he rubbed his whole body against Vex's legs, around and around, purring like a motorbike.
Vex stared down at him.
"He never does that," said Ela. "Paşa hates everybody. He hates *me.*"
"He says," said Bora slowly, "that Vex smells like Grandma. Like her tea. He says Vex has been near her. Recently." Bora looked at Vex. "He wants to know if she's okay."
Vex knelt down, very slowly, on the kitchen floor. He put out his human hand, his left one, and Paşa pushed his head into it.
"She's okay," Vex said quietly, to the cat. "She's knitting. She talks about you. She worries about who's feeding you."
Paşa purred louder.
Ela put her hand on my shoulder.
"She'll be back here," she said. "Soon. We'll make sure."
I went to the stove. I filled the kettle. I lit the gas.
And I waited. Until it started to hum. And then to whistle. And steam poured out of the spout and filled the kitchen with a soft warm cloud.
"There," I said. "Now it's a kitchen again."
Behind me, I heard Vera laugh. A small, wet laugh.
§END To be continued in* The Gate of Seven Winds...
